mcqs.question: Why does the viewer fan-out ratio matter more for capacity planning than the streamer's ingest bitrate?
options: A single low-bitrate ingest stream can fan out to egress that is orders of magnitude larger once multiplied across many concurrent viewers at their own bitrates
Ingest bitrate is always higher than total viewer egress in practice
Viewer count has no effect on total bandwidth required
Ingest and egress bandwidth are always provisioned from the same fixed budget
mcqs.explanation: A 6Mbps ingest stream feeding 100,000 viewers at ~3Mbps each is 300Gbps of egress — the multiplication by viewer count is what dominates, not the single ingest stream. Ingest is typically far smaller than aggregate egress, viewer count is exactly what drives total bandwidth, and ingest/egress are provisioned and scaled independently.

mcqs.question: Why do live streaming platforms use much shorter segments than VOD platforms?
options: Short segments always improve CDN cache hit rates compared to long ones
Every second of segment length adds directly to end-to-end latency, which live platforms are actively trying to minimize; VOD has no such latency pressure
Long segments are technically incompatible with HLS and DASH
Live streams always have lower total bitrate than VOD, requiring smaller segments
mcqs.explanation: In live, each second of segment length is a second the viewer sits further behind the true live moment, so segments shrink to protect the latency budget. VOD has no such pressure and prefers larger segments for delivery efficiency. Cache hit rate isn't the driver here, both protocols support various segment sizes, and bitrate isn't inherently lower for live.

mcqs.question: Why does a transcode backlog behave differently in live streaming than in VOD?
options: In live streaming a transcode backlog is instantly visible to every current viewer as added latency or stutter, while VOD's backlog only delays publish for a video nobody is watching yet
Transcode backlogs are impossible in a live streaming system by design
VOD backlogs are always worse than live backlogs in every scenario
Live transcode backlogs only affect the streamer, never the viewers
mcqs.explanation: This option is deliberately backwards to test careful reading: a live backlog is exactly what hits viewers directly and simultaneously, since there's no queue to absorb it — the opposite of what this wrong option claims. VOD's backlog is comparatively low-stakes since it only delays a video before anyone is watching; live backlogs absolutely are possible and do hit viewers, not just the streamer.

mcqs.question: What's the core mistake in treating a live streaming platform as 'VOD that publishes sooner'?
options: VOD pipelines cannot technically process live ingest streams at all
Live viewers don't actually care about latency, so the distinction is unnecessary
It ignores that live content doesn't exist ahead of time, so every hop — transcode, distribution, cache warm — must happen within the live latency budget instead of before any viewer request
Live streaming requires an entirely different video codec than VOD
mcqs.explanation: VOD's design leans on the video already existing, letting transcode and cache-warming happen with no viewer waiting; live has no such luxury — everything must happen within seconds. Latency is precisely what live viewers notice and care about; the codec itself can be shared between VOD and live; and VOD infrastructure can technically ingest a live feed, it's just architected for the wrong latency assumptions.
